\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}

\title{TinySet: Admission Control for Small-Object Caches at the Edge}
\author{R.~Petrova, J.~Lindgren, and M.~Osei}
\date{July 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Edge caches that serve small objects waste much of their capacity on
items requested only once. We describe an admission control scheme
that filters one-hit wonders with a compact counting structure, and
we evaluate it on production traces from three points of presence.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
A large fraction of objects requested at the edge are fetched exactly
once during any measurement window. Admitting such objects into a
small cache displaces content that would have been reused, and the
resulting miss traffic falls on links that are often the bottleneck
of the whole delivery path.

Admission control addresses this problem at the moment an object is
first requested. Rather than caching every missed object, the cache
admits only objects that have demonstrated some likelihood of reuse.
The design space is wide, and Section~\ref{sec:eval} later compares
several points in it on production traces.

Prior schemes either remember too much about past requests or react
too slowly to shifting popularity. The scheme described here keeps a
fixed-size probabilistic sketch whose error behaviour is independent
of the trace length, a property we exploit heavily in what follows.

\section{Design}
The cache front-end maintains a counting sketch of recent request
keys. On a miss, the front-end consults the sketch and admits the
object only if its estimated count exceeds a threshold. The sketch is
aged periodically by halving all counters, which bounds the memory of
the estimator without any explicit eviction bookkeeping.

The threshold is not free: a higher threshold filters more one-hit
wonders but also delays the admission of objects whose popularity is
genuinely rising. We expose the threshold as a single knob and derive
a default from the miss-ratio curves of the training traces.

Two implementation details matter at line rate. First, sketch updates
must complete within the per-packet budget of the front-end pipeline.
Second, the halving pass must not stall lookups, so aging is performed
incrementally across ordinary requests rather than in a batch.

\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:eval}
We replay three production traces, totalling 41 days of requests,
through a simulator that reproduces the front-end pipeline exactly.
The baseline admits every missed object; the comparison schemes cover
the two dominant prior designs. All schemes are given the same memory
budget, including the memory our sketch consumes.

The proposed scheme reduces byte miss ratio by 31 percent relative to
the baseline at the median, and by 18 percent relative to the stronger
prior design. Gains concentrate in the traces with the heaviest tail
of single-request objects, as the design discussion anticipated.

Sensitivity to the threshold is modest within a factor of two of the
derived default, which supports the claim that the knob need not be
retuned per deployment. The incremental aging pass adds no measurable
lookup latency at the 95th percentile.

\section{Conclusion}
Filtering at admission is a cheap and effective lever for small-object
caches, and a fixed-size sketch makes the filter practical at line
rate. The remaining question is how admission control interacts with
prefetching policies that already shape edge traffic, which we leave
to future work.

\end{document}
